books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, A. Slave Rebellions
Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, 1829

stimulus.text: "Let no man of us budge one step, and let slave-holders come to beat us from our country. America is more our country, than it is the whites—we have enriched it with our blood and tears." — David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, September 28, 1829
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (Boston, September 28, 1829). Wording checked against the Documenting the American South electronic edition.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from David Walker (1829)
stem: Walker calls America “more our country” than the whites’. That claim rests mainly on which of the following?

options.text: The Constitution had already granted Black Americans full citizenship
options.misconception: Walker argues Black Americans have earned a claim to the country, not that the law already gives it to them.

options.text: Black Americans should leave the United States for Africa
options.misconception: Walker says the opposite: let no man of us budge one step.

options.text: Black labor built American wealth, giving Black Americans a claim to it
White Americans had invited Black workers to share the country equally
options.misconception: Walker speaks of slaveholders beating Black people from their homes, not of an invitation.

rationales.A: Walker never says the Constitution granted Black Americans citizenship. He argues they have earned a claim to the country.
rationales.B: Walker says the opposite: “Let no man of us budge one step.” Leaving for Africa is the plan he rejects.
rationales.C: Walker says Black Americans enriched America with their blood and tears. That labor is his proof that the country belongs to them too.
rationales.D: Nothing in the passage shows white Americans inviting Black workers to share the country. Walker speaks of beatings and driving out.
rationales.general:
1. Find Walker’s proof. He does not point to a law. He points to blood and tears, the labor that enriched America.
2. Ask what the proof is meant to win. Walker wants Black Americans to stay and claim the country as their own.
3. Rule out leaving. “Let no man of us budge one step” rejects the colonization plan outright.
Background: Walker published the Appeal in Boston in 1829, and Southern states soon banned it.
Remember: when a writer says “we built this,” ask what right the building is meant to prove.
